Carbon footprint: High CO₂: cotton cultivation and processing drive ≈2.6 % of global water withdrawals and require energy-intensive cultivation, ginning and finishing
endOfLife: Most post-consumer cotton ends up exported or incinerated; only ≈1 % is closed-loop-recycled in Europe
sourcing: Plant-based, but pesticide- and land-intensive; switch to hemp/flax suggested
waterUse: Very water-thirsty: the fibre is singled-out as “highest water use compared with other materials”
citation: Mapping Textile Waste Flows Towards Its Potential for Recycling. Ponnet, 2024.

Carbon footprint: Large fossil-carbon footprint (> 100 MJ kg-¹ virgin production) and responsible for micro-plastic shed during washing
endOfLife: Only 1 % of garments are remade into new ones; most flow is exported, incinerated or used for energy recovery
sourcing: Petroleum-derived, though bottle-to-fibre recycling is rising (~15 % of PET fibre)
waterUse: Lower process-water demand than cotton
citation: Mapping Textile Waste Flows Towards Its Potential for Recycling. Ponnet, 2024.

Carbon footprint: Moderate CO₂ (lower than polyester if pulp is sustainably sourced)
endOfLife: Same linear fate as other fibres; chemical recycling routes are still niche
sourcing: Wood-pulp feedstock is renewable but “unsustainably sourced” in many supply chains; new fast-growing crops & closed-loop solvents recommended
waterUse: Process water significant (dissolving & washing) yet below cotton; improvement relies on solvent recovery
citation: Mapping Textile Waste Flows Towards Its Potential for Recycling. Ponnet, 2024.

Carbon footprint: Not quantified in detail, but table flags biodegradable, flame-retardant fibre; environmental pressure comes from land & methane
endOfLife: Shares the same low-recycling, high-export/incineration profile of Belgian waste streams
sourcing: Animal fibre; extensive land requirement but low agro-chemical input
waterUse: Water use lower than cotton, higher than synthetics (scouring)
citation: Mapping Textile Waste Flows Towards Its Potential for Recycling. Ponnet, 2024.

Carbon footprint: High process-energy emissions: cradle-to-gate LCAs of finished bovine leather flag tanning and finishing as the dominant global-warming hotspots
endOfLife: Still largely linear—most post-consumer leather is land-filled or incinerated; studies urge a shift to recycling to recover embedded resources
sourcing: Bovine hides are slaughter-house by-products, yet traceability (animal welfare, farm origin) is a growing concern as production migrates to emerging economies
waterUse: Beamhouse operations and chrome tanning drive a substantial water footprint; Mexican case studies single them out as the main water consumers
citation: Life Cycle Assessment and Leather Production. Navarro et al., 2020.

Carbon footprint: High-mid range: cradle-to-gate averages around 25 kg CO₂-eq kg-¹ of garment because of the energy used to rear silkworms, boil cocoons and spin filament
endOfLife: 100 % biodegradable but little is actually composted; garments mostly incinerated or land-filled like other apparel
sourcing: Mulberry sericulture in China & India; land is chemical-light but requires large amounts of fuelwood/steam for reeling
waterUse: Processing water moderate, well below cotton
citation: Carbon Footprints in the Textile Industry. Peters et al., 2015.

Carbon footprint: Lower than most naturals: ≈15 kg CO₂-eq kg-¹ due to mechanical fibre retting & low-input farming
endOfLife: Readily biodegradable; EU studies show > 80 % post-consumer linen still goes to landfill/incineration; mechanical recycling feasible but niche
sourcing: European rain-fed flax; little agro-chemical input; straw coproduct for bio-energy adds circular value
waterUse: Very low irrigation; scutching & wet-spinning use < 20 % of cotton’s process water
citation: Carbon Footprints in the Textile Industry. Peters et al., 2015.

Carbon footprint: Cradle-to-gate among the highest for textiles (≈ 35-38 kg CO₂-eq kg-¹) because of fossil-based acrylonitrile & solvent-intensive wet-spinning
endOfLife: Thermoplastic, seldom recycled; most garments incinerated for energy recovery (high calorific value)
sourcing: Petroleum feedstock via propylene–acrylonitrile route; relies on ammonia & HCN—tightening regulations raise supply-chain risk
waterUse: Minimal process water; no field phase
citation: Carbon Footprints in the Textile Industry. Peters et al., 2015.

Carbon footprint: Mid-high: ≈ 24 kg CO₂-eq kg-¹ (PA 6) with key hotspots in caprolactam production & energy-hungry melt-spinning
endOfLife: Chemical recycling (e.g., Aquafil) is scaling but still < 5 %; bulk of apparel nylon is land-filled or incinerated
sourcing: Petrochemical feedstock; emerging bio-adipic acid could cut upstream GHGs
waterUse: Low water demand throughout synthetic route
citation: Carbon Footprints in the Textile Industry. Peters et al., 2015.

Carbon footprint: Lowest fossil synthetics assessed: ≈ 15 kg CO₂-eq kg-¹ woven PP
endOfLife: Easily melt-recyclable and widely collected in industrial streams; consumer textile recycling still rare
sourcing: Derived from propylene (steam-cracker by-product); high global oversupply keeps prices & impact down
waterUse: Negligible process water
citation: Carbon Footprints in the Textile Industry. Peters et al., 2015.

Carbon footprint: Around 20 kg CO₂-eq kg-¹ for garments—polyol & isocyanate synthesis are energy-intensive and release N₂O
endOfLife: Cannot be mechanically recycled; landfill & incineration dominate; R&D on chemolysis still pilot-scale
sourcing: Oil-based polyols & MDI/TDI; increasingly sourced from Asia; bio-based PU (< 10 %) emerging but marginal
waterUse: Very low direct water use; solvent/DMF clean-up drives EHS risk rather than water footprint
citation: Carbon Footprints in the Textile Industry. Peters et al., 2015.

Carbon footprint: Full LCA shows 0.63 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ on average (0.10–0.90 kg range depending on waste stream and treatment), ~60 % lower than virgin wool and even in the worst case still < 1 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹
endOfLife: Made entirely from pre- & post-consumer wool waste; garments can repeat the mechanical cycle several times before fibre shortening limits quality, but today most still end up land-filled/incinerated after use despite the circular potential
sourcing: 85 % post-consumer clothing from the USA/N-Europe and 15 % pre-consumer scraps; sorted in India/Pakistan, shipped to Italy, then frayed or shredded—so no new sheep farming inputs and the feedstock is classed “burden-free” waste
waterUse: Net water deprivation is 0.093 m³ kg⁻¹, a tiny fraction of virgin wool’s ~13.9 m³; 16 % of this comes from wet shredding, the rest from background electricity and transport
citation: Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) of MWool® Recycled Wool Fibers. Bianco et al., 2022.

Carbon footprint: LCAs show a broad range: 78–97 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ for fine worsted yarns and 25–30 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ for coarser woollen fibers; in every case, sheep grazing dominates (≈ 89 % of GHGs)
endOfLife: Post-consumer wool garments remain overwhelmingly linear—reuse and closed-loop recycling are niche, so landfill or incineration is typical
sourcing: Derived from sheep raised mainly in Australia, China and New Zealand; the grazing phase drives impacts through enteric methane, land occupation and feed inputs
waterUse: Process-water deprivation for spinning/finishing averages 13–18 m³ kg⁻¹ for worsted routes, slightly lower (~ 12 m³ kg⁻¹) for belly-wool streams
citation: Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) of Worsted and Woollen Processing in Wool Production. Bianco et al., 2023.

Carbon footprint: 100 % r-PET denim shows ≈ 3.95 kg CO₂-eq per metre (≈ 11 kg kg⁻¹ fabric)—about 20 % lower than a cotton-rich reference and 30 % below virgin PET denim; most gains come from avoiding virgin resin production
endOfLife: Garments still largely land-filled/incinerated, yet feedstock already came from post-consumer bottles, so closed-loop potential is higher if textile-to-textile recycling scales
sourcing: Feedstock = shredded PET drink bottles collected, washed and re-melt-spun in Turkey; eliminates upstream oil use but adds long-haul transport burdens if bottles are imported
waterUse: Factory-gate water demand 0.062 m³ m⁻¹ fabric, ≈ 55 % lower than cotton reference and 60 % below virgin PET denim
citation: Sustainability assessment of denim fabric made of PET fiber and recycled fiber from postconsumer PET bottles using LCA and LCC approach with the EDAS method. Fidan et al., 2024.

Carbon footprint: Virgin-PET denim scores ≈ 5.62 kg CO₂-eq m⁻¹ (≈ 15 kg kg⁻¹)—~ 15 % higher than cotton-rich baseline and 42 % higher than r-PET; bottle-grade resin and melt spinning dominate GHGs
endOfLife: Textile recycling < 5 %; most garments head to landfill or energy-recovery incineration, with micro-plastic shed during use
sourcing: Petroleum-derived ethylene/para-xylene → PTA/EG → PET chips; energy-intensive polymerisation and filament spinning
waterUse: Water consumption 0.165 m³ m⁻¹, the highest of the three scenarios because of cooling and wash processes
citation: Sustainability assessment of denim fabric made of PET fiber and recycled fiber from postconsumer PET bottles using LCA and LCC approach with the EDAS method. Fidan et al., 2024.

Carbon footprint: 4.88 kg CO₂-eq m⁻¹ (≈ 13 kg kg⁻¹); cultivation (diesel, N-fertiliser) and rope-dyeing steam drive emissions
endOfLife: Only ~ 1 % enters closed-loop fibre recycling; biodegrades if composted but most ends in landfill/incineration
sourcing: Field-grown (Turkey), high fertiliser & pesticide inputs; relies on irrigation where rainfall is insufficient
waterUse: 0.139 m³ m⁻¹—more than double r-PET and 16 % below virgin PET; driven by crop irrigation and wet processing
citation: Sustainability assessment of denim fabric made of PET fiber and recycled fiber from postconsumer PET bottles using LCA and LCC approach with the EDAS method. Fidan et al., 2024.

Carbon footprint: LCAs of glass-fiber/epoxy parts show the fiber itself contributes ~ 28 % of composite GWP; at a typical 5 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ composite this scales to ≈ 1–2 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ glass fiber (≈ 40/100)
endOfLife: Thermoset glass-fiber composites are “difficult to recycle and may be a potential landfill problem,” so most post-consumer waste is still land-filled or incinerated (≈ 30/100)
sourcing: Made from abundant silica sand, but melting at > 1600 °C is highly energy-intensive; however, no farmland, irrigation or agro-chemicals are required (≈ 50/100)
waterUse: The melt-spinning process is essentially dry; water demand is limited to closed-loop cooling systems, giving a smaller water footprint than most natural fibers (< 0.05 m³ kg⁻¹, ≈ 60/100)
citation: LCA of fibre-reinforced composites, Cicala & Lo Faro, 2015

Carbon footprint: • Fibre = 3.3 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ • Fabric = 8.3 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ • Full FR coverall ≈ 58 kg CO₂-eq (lower than cotton, ≈ = modacrylic)
endOfLife: Non-biodegradable; garments typically land-filled or incinerated, adding another ≈ 58 kg CO₂-eq and leaving persistent micro-plastic residues
sourcing: Fully synthetic; polymerised from petro-chemical monomers (meta-phenylenediamine + isophthaloyl chloride) in solvent-intensive spinning—wholly fossil-based, energy-intensive processes
waterUse: Process-water mostly from wet-finishing; generic textile average ~ 164 L kg⁻¹—well below cotton but still significant for wastewater treatment
citation: Life Cycle Assessment of Flame-Resistant Textiles Used in the Production of Occupational Safety Clothing: A Focus on the Personal Protective Equipment Industry. Ikimi, 2024.

Carbon footprint: Very low cradle-to-gate CO₂: field phase ≈ 0.15 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ and yarn production ≈ 1.4 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹—lowest of the six fibres studied
endOfLife: Biodegradable bast fibre, but > 70 % of jute textiles still end up land-filled or incinerated; true closed-loop recycling remains niche
sourcing: Rain-fed crop grown mainly in India/Bangladesh; minimal fertiliser and pesticide inputs, giving the best fossil-resource-scarcity score among fibres
waterUse: Tiny footprint: cultivation uses just 0.057 m³ kg⁻¹ and the full spinning route totals ≈ 0.27 m³ kg⁻¹—an order of magnitude below cotton
citation: Evaluating Environmental Impact of Natural and Synthetic fibers: A Life Cycle Assessment Approach. Gonzalez et al., 2023.

Carbon footprint: Fibre production emits ≈ 4.7 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ (net ≈ 3 kg after photosynthetic uptake) and needs 59.8 MJ kg⁻¹—about 40 % less energy than polyester, yet hotel sheets still demand more energy overall because two cotton sheets are needed to match the lifetime of one CO/PES sheet
endOfLife: Biodegradable, but most garments are still land-filled or incinerated; landfill decomposition creates CH₄/CO₂, while incineration can reclaim ~ 20 MJ kg⁻¹ heat
sourcing: Field crop grown largely in water-scarce regions; irrigation 7 – 29 m³ kg⁻¹ fibre and high agro-chemical inputs (≈ 457 g fertiliser, 16 g pesticide kg⁻¹) raise ecotoxicity concerns
waterUse: Very water-intensive: cultivation and processing together consume ≈ 22 000 – 52 000 L kg⁻¹ fibre, > 99 % of which is on-farm irrigation
citation: Life Cycle Assessment: Environmental Profile of Cotton and Polyester Cotton Fabrics. Kalliala & Nousiainen, 1999.

Carbon footprint: ISO-14067 LCA gives 6.0 t CO₂-eq for 3 500 m, i.e. 1.72 kg CO₂-eq m⁻¹ (≈ 4.8 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ assuming 360 g m⁻²) cradle-to-gate
endOfLife: Fibre-blend makes mechanical/chemical separation uneconomic; most garments are still land-filled or incinerated, with only niche open-loop routes available
sourcing: ~ 45 % sheep wool (enteric-methane, pasture land) + ~ 55 % virgin PET from fossil oil; high-temperature melt-spinning and farm emissions dominate impacts
waterUse: Facility relies on on-site wells; dye-finishing is water-intensive but volumes not reported—typical textile wet-processing uses ≈ 45 – 200 L kg⁻¹ cloth, suggesting a lower footprint than cotton but higher than synthetic-only fabrics
citation: A Life Cycle Analysis of a Polyester–Wool Blended Fabric and Associated Carbon Emissions in the Textile Industry. Tekin et al., 2024.

Carbon footprint: Cradle-to-gate ≈ 21 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ for typical garments (e.g., 2.55 kg CO₂-eq for a 130 g T-shirt) and ≈ 10 kg CO₂-eq cradle-to-grave for a 0.48 kg dress; in a detailed LCA of a 100 % knit blouse, consumer laundering drives 82 % of life-cycle energy (1.6 GJ per 10⁶ wearings)
endOfLife: Non-biodegradable; most post-consumer items landfilled or incinerated (39 % of life-cycle solid-waste volume comes at the disposal stage). Mechanical (rPET) and emerging chemical recycling can recapture fibre value, but current capture rates remain low
sourcing: Virgin PET is made from petroleum/natural-gas aromatics, requiring ~ 97 MJ kg⁻¹ of primary energy and < 3 kg non-renewable feedstocks; recycled PET (bottle or textile) can cut these inputs by ~ 30-50 %
waterUse: Production water demand is very low (~ 17 L kg⁻¹ fibre vs > 20 000 L kg⁻¹ cotton) , but user washing dominates the life-cycle, accounting for 44-60 % of total garment water consumption
citation: Prospective Environmental Life Cycle Asssessment of Nanosilver T-shirts, Walser et al. 2011 and  Life Cycle Analysis of a Polyester Garment. Smith & Barker, 1995.

Carbon footprint: Base fibre ≈ 3.5 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹; spinning (70 dtex) + weaving together add a further ~ 9 kg, making cotton the highest-impact fibre in the study
endOfLife: In Western Europe ~ 67 % of garments are energy-recovery-incinerated, 33 % collected for reuse/down-cycling; cotton receives a small CO₂ credit when burnt because the carbon is biogenic
sourcing: Cultivation data modelled for Chinese farms (“cotton fibres, ginned, at farm/CN”)
waterUse: Wet-processing steps for cotton (desizing, scouring, etc.) can consume 200 – 450 L kg⁻¹ fabric, and this omits on-farm irrigation, so overall water pressure is the highest among fibres considered
citation: LCA Benchmarking Study on Textiles made of Cotton,Polyester, Nylon, Acryl, or Elastane. van der Velden et al., 2014.

Carbon footprint: Virgin pellets ≈ 2.7 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹; even after extrusion and weaving it remains one of the lower-impact options among synthetics
endOfLife: Same disposal profile as other synthetics; today most PET textiles are incinerated or land-filled, with only niche mechanical/chemical recycling
sourcing: Modelled as “polyethylene terephthalate, amorphous granulate, at plant/RER” — fossil feedstock, European production
waterUse: Study focuses on energy, not water, but typical dyeing/finishing for synthetics falls in the 45 – 200 L kg⁻¹ range, far below cotton and with no field irrigation
citation: LCA Benchmarking Study on Textiles made of Cotton,Polyester, Nylon, Acryl, or Elastane. van der Velden et al., 2014.

Carbon footprint: Highest of the five polymers assessed: ≈ 8.6 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ polymer pellets; nylon woven at 70 dtex ranks just behind cotton in overall burden
endOfLife: Non-biodegradable; majority incinerated/land-filled, limited fibre-to-fibre recycling; no heat-recovery credit like cotton
sourcing: Blend of 50 % PA 6 and 50 % PA 66 produced at European plants (RER)
waterUse: Water in mill processing similar to PET (≈ 45 – 200 L kg⁻¹); no agricultural irrigation
citation: LCA Benchmarking Study on Textiles made of Cotton,Polyester, Nylon, Acryl, or Elastane. van der Velden et al., 2014.

Carbon footprint: Polyurethane fibre ≈ 4.8 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ (mid-range); when blended, it raises the impact of fabrics relative to PET but below nylon
endOfLife: Adds stretch but complicates recycling; garments follow the same linear path (incineration > land-fill)
sourcing: “Polyurethane, flexible foam, at plant/RER” — entirely fossil-based synthesis
waterUse: Process-water loads align with other synthetics (≈ 45 – 200 L kg⁻¹); no cultivation phase
citation: LCA Benchmarking Study on Textiles made of Cotton,Polyester, Nylon, Acryl, or Elastane. van der Velden et al., 2014.

Carbon footprint: No CO₂ figure given; process innovations cut carbon-disulfide use by 30.5 % and remove bleaching/ageing, signalling a lower cradle-to-gate impact than conventional viscose
endOfLife: Establishes a genuine fibre-to-fibre loop by turning pre-consumer viscose waste into new staple; final garments can still be land-filled or incinerated if textile-to-textile collection is lacking
sourcing: Feedstock is 100 % pre-consumer undyed viscose off-cuts—avoids virgin wood pulp and the forestry footprint, relying mainly on mechanical defibration plus double-steeping chemistry
waterUse: Study lists multiple closed-loop washes (e.g., H₂SO₄ 18 g L⁻¹ at 90 °C) but does not quantify total m³ kg⁻¹; elimination of irrigation (wood-growing) and fewer chemical baths suggests a moderate footprint
citation: Towards Sustainable Viscose-to-Viscose Production: Strategiesfor Recycling of Viscose Fibres. Forsberg et al., 2024.

Carbon footprint: 14.6 kg CO₂-eq cradle-to-gate (average hemp yarn)
endOfLife: 100 % cellulose → readily biodegradable or mechanically recyclable into staple fibre. Industrial composting or fibre-to-fibre recycling feasible; no hazardous residues.
sourcing: Annual bast crop; grows quickly with little or no synthetic fertilizer/pesticides and can be cultivated on marginal land.
waterUse: Requires far less irrigation than cotton; typical yields 1–5 t ha⁻¹ with minimal water inputs
citation: Systematic Insights into a Textile Industry: Reviewing Life Cycle Assessment and Eco-Design. Fonseca et al., 2023.

Carbon footprint: 30.1 kg CO₂-eq cradle-to-grave (average modal garment)
endOfLife: Cellulosic fibre is biodegradable and can be chemically recycled back to dissolving pulp; incineration with energy recovery common where composting not available.
sourcing: Sourced from sustainably managed beech forests; solvent-spinning (viscose-type) process in closed loops recovers > 99 % of chemicals.
waterUse: Closed-loop spinning uses ~ 50 % less water than conventional viscose; far lower field irrigation than cotton (forest-based).
citation: Systematic Insights into a Textile Industry: Reviewing Life Cycle Assessment and Eco-Design. Fonseca et al., 2023.

Carbon footprint: Mechanical closed-loop route for a 178 g T-shirt: 3.43 kg CO₂-eq per life-cycle, 13 % lower than the virgin/linear counterpart (3.56 kg)
endOfLife: 60 % of worn shirts are separately collected; mechanical shredding recovers 27 % of the original fibre, the rest is still land-filled / incinerated
sourcing: Feedstock = post-consumer cotton from Norway, shredded in Lithuania, respun in China—so ≈ 27 % less virgin cotton and farm inputs than the linear system
waterUse: Total cradle-to-grave water demand 1.28 m³ per shirt, 13 % below the linear cotton route (1.47 m³) because no new irrigation is needed for the recovered portion
citation: Sustainable Clothing Systems: A Comparative Life Cycle Assessment of T-Shirts Made from Primary and Recycled Materials. Ahmed, 2024.

Carbon footprint: Chemical depolymerisation + re-granulation gives ≈ 6.66 kg CO₂-eq per shirt, only 0.5 % lower than the virgin route (6.69 kg) because virgin PET accounts for < 15 % of total impact
endOfLife: 29 % of PET is recovered as DMT / EG and re-used; extra transport, sorting and chemistry offset much of the benefit, so most garments still end up in energy-recovery incineration
sourcing: 46 g of recycled PET chips displace virgin granulate; balance (71 %) remains fossil-based. Feedstock bottles/textiles are chemically split, re-polymerised and spun in China
waterUse: Water footprint unchanged at ≈ 0.06 m³ per shirt (wet processing + use phase dominate)
citation: Sustainable Clothing Systems: A Comparative Life Cycle Assessment of T-Shirts Made from Primary and Recycled Materials. Ahmed, 2024.

Carbon footprint: ≈ 0.55 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ cradle-to-gate—about 80 % lower than PP fabric and one-fifth that of cotton; main hotspots are field diesel and baling electricity
endOfLife: 100 % lignocellulosic → compostable or mechanically recycled to staple; today most kenaf textiles still end up land-filled or incinerated, though no toxic residues form
sourcing: Bast fiber from Hibiscus cannabinus grown in India/Bangladesh; rain-fed, minimal pesticide/fertilizer inputs; fibre often retted in the same ponds used for jute, giving a by-product use pathway
waterUse: ≈ 0.70 m³ kg⁻¹ cradle-to-gate. Field phase is largely rain-fed; water is mainly for pond-retting and mill washing—~ 10 × lower than cotton but higher than PP and glass fiber
citation: Comparative analysis of carbon, ecological, and water footprints of polypropylene-based composites filled with cotton, jute and kenaf fibers. Korol et al., 2020.

Carbon footprint: Cradle-to-gate 3.43 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹; > 84 % of that comes from grid electricity and the propylene monomer, with CO₂ making up > 90 % of GHGs
endOfLife: Thermoplastic and readily melt-recyclable, yet most consumer PP textiles still follow a linear path to energy-recovery incineration or landfill (the EUR-pallet case assumes no post-use recycling)
sourcing: Derived entirely from fossil propylene; electricity plus monomer production dominate all three footprints
waterUse: 0.059 m³ kg⁻¹ (≈ 59 L) — largely cooling water tied to electricity generation; far below natural fibres but higher than glass fiber
citation: Comparative analysis of carbon, ecological, and water footprints of polypropylene-based composites filled with cotton, jute and kenaf fibers. Korol et al., 2020.

Carbon footprint: Extensive-grazing LCA (Peruvian Andes) reports 53 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ greasy fibre (biophysical allocation); enteric-methane is 67 % of total GHGs
endOfLife: Fully biodegradable protein fibre, but post-consumer garments are still overwhelmingly land-filled or incinerated; fibre-to-fibre recycling remains niche
sourcing: Herders raise alpacas on high-Andean grasslands with almost no external feed, fertiliser, or energy inputs—low resource intensity but high methane intensity
waterUse: Water footprint not quantified; system relies on natural rainfall for pasture, with no irrigation or wet-processing at farm gate—implying a very low blue-water demand
citation: Estimation of carbon footprint and sources of emissions of an extensive alpaca production system. Gómez Oquendo et al., 2022.

Carbon footprint: Fabrication of 1 m² cellulose-triacetate UF membrane in France emits ≈ 11 kg CO₂-eq (IPCC 100a) – energy for solvent (NMP) production and glycerol pre-conditioning dominate
endOfLife: Cellulose backbone is compostable once fully de-acetylated, but in practice most acetate textiles and membranes are land-filled or incinerated; fibre-to-fibre recycling is still at pilot scale
sourcing: Wood-pulp feedstock acetylated with acetic anhydride; solvent-intensive NIPS route relies on N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) and glycerol, so impacts hinge on certified forestry and greener solvent choices
waterUse: Process inventory lists ≈ 144 L water m⁻² (117 kg tap + 26.6 kg softened) – orders-of-magnitude lower than cotton but higher than melt-spun synthetics
citation: A generic Process Modelling – LCA approach for UF Membrane Fabrication: Application to Cellulose Acetate Membranes. Prézélus et al., 2020.

Carbon footprint: ≈ 3.5 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ – about 25 % lower than fossil-PU thanks to rapeseed-oil polyol, with lower CED in 8 of 18 ReCiPe mid-point categories
endOfLife: Cross-linked thermoset: mechanical recycling limited; typically landfilled or energy-recovered. Highly resistant to hydrolysis/UV/washing and passes ISO 15025, so unlikely to biodegrade quickly
sourcing: ~ 60 % bio-carbon from fatty-acid polyester polyol; water-borne process (no DMF); still uses petro-isocyanate & catalysts
waterUse: No blue-water figure given; coating formulated in water carrier with minimal process water—overall demand expected low; upstream irrigation depends on oil-crop feedstock
citation: Bio-based waterborne PU for durable textile coatings. De Smet et al., 2021.

Carbon footprint: ~ 2.8 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ cradle-to-gate (conversion step alone ≈ 2.8 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹ and > 50 % of total; biogenic uptake ≈ 1.8 kg CO₂ kg⁻¹ can lower net impact)
endOfLife: Industrial composting, mechanical & chemical recycling; recycling cuts GHG 0.3–1.2 × versus incineration, but infrastructure still limited
sourcing: Renewable feedstocks (corn, sugarcane). Conversion relies heavily on fossil energy—natural gas 65 %, electricity 22 % per kg PLA
waterUse: Review flags “water resources usage” as a significant impact but gives no figure; LCAs place process-water demand in the low-moderate range (≈ 0.05–0.10 m³ kg⁻¹, largely from agriculture & fermentation)
citation: The Life Cycle Assessment for Polylactic Acid (PLA) to Make it a Low-Carbon Material. Rezvani Ghomi et al., 2021.

Carbon footprint: LCA of European warm-water retting: 1 350 kg CO₂-eq per 100 kg yarn ⇒ 13.5 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹
endOfLife: Fully biodegradable; garments still mainly land-filled/incinerated; fibre-to-fibre recycling remains niche
sourcing: Bast crop grown without pesticides in Central Europe; retting pools use naturally heated thermal water; diesel & fertiliser are minor hotspots
waterUse: 19.9 m³ per 100 kg yarn (≈ 199 L kg⁻¹) from retting + bleaching—~ 3 × flax, still < 1 % of cotton irrigation
citation: The Environmental Impacts of the Production of Hemp and Flax Textile Yarn. van der Werf & Turunen, 2008.

Carbon footprint: Dew-retting scenario: 1 360 kg CO₂-eq per 100 kg yarn ⇒ 13.6 kg CO₂-eq kg⁻¹—very similar to hemp
endOfLife: Biodegradable; higher reuse rates than hemp but most garments still incinerated/land-filled; limited closed-loop spinning
sourcing: Western-European flax grown without irrigation; higher pesticide use than hemp but far higher long-fibre yield (≈ 62 % of stem mass)
waterUse: 7.23 m³ per 100 kg yarn (≈ 72 L kg⁻¹) — only bleaching water; no retting liquor to treat
citation: The Environmental Impacts of the Production of Hemp and Flax Textile Yarn. van der Werf & Turunen, 2008.
